newsitem.title: USA: Royal Dutch/Shell tops Forbes' global list.
newsitem.headline: Royal Dutch/Shell tops Forbes' global list.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch Oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group took first place in Forbes magazine's annual ranking of the 50 most powerful public companies in the world for the third year in a row -- but U.S. corporations dominated the list.

U.S. companies made up half of the "World Super 50" ranking in the July 28 issue of the business magazine hitting newsstands Monday. Among them were General Electric Co, which placed second, Exxon Corp (No. 3) and computer giant International Business Machines Corp. (No. 4).
U.S. companies also making the top 10 were automakers Ford Motor Co in sixth place and General Motors Corp, seventh, as well as retailer Wal-Mart Stores Inc, ninth.

After Royal Dutch/Shell, the top-ranking non-U.S. company on the Super 50 was automaker Toyota Motor Corp at fifth place. Rounding out the top 10 were British Petroleum Co Plc in eighth and the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, which tied Wal-Mart for ninth.

Forbes said the Super 50 was compiled by first combining the Forbes Foreign 500, the July 28 issue's ranking of the 500 biggest non-U.S. public companies by sales and its Forbes Sales 500, the 500 biggest U.S. companies by sales.

The magazine then assigned those companies scores based on the best three of four ranks for sales, profits, assets and market value. That meant a company could qualify for the Super 50 if its profits declined but it scored well in the other three areas.

Japanese trading houses dominated the top spots in the Forbes Foreign 500. Mitsui & Co Ltd took first place with $144 billion in revenues, Mitsubishi Corp came second with $140.2 billion, and third was Itochu Corp ($135.5 billion).

Royal Dutch/Shell took fourth place with $128.2 billion in sales. Japanese companies formed the remainder of the top 10, with trading houses Marubeni Corp and Sumitomo Corp in fifth and sixth place, respectively.
Bringing up the rear were automaker Toyota Motor, trading house Nissho Iwai Corp, telecommunications giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp and electronics colossus Hitachi Ltd.

Japan is home to 195, or 39 percent, of the 500 foreign companies that made Forbes' cut, with Britain in second place with 67 companies. In third was France, with 46 companies, followed by Germany, with 40, the Netherlands (19), Switzerland and Canada (16 each), South Korea and Italy (15 each) and Australia and Sweden (13 each).
Some companies, including Royal Dutch/Shell and consumer products conglomerate Unilever Plc, were counted as being in two countries because they claim dual headquarters.

The Forbes Foreign 500 earned $208 billion on $7.9 trillion in revenues in the most recent fiscal year, compared with $295 billion on $4.8 trillion in revenues for their U.S counterparts in the Forbes Sales 500, the magazine said. So, U.S. firms earned $87 billion more than the 500 non-U.S. companies did on a little more than 60 percent of the total sales.

Companies considered for the Foreign 500 had to be publicly traded as of May 30, 1997, Forbes said. The magazine looked at companies' most recent fiscal years ending between June 1996 and May 1997. It used average currency exchange rates in converting financial results to U.S. dollars, using the rate prevaling at the end of a company's fiscal year.
Forbes' July 28 issue also lists the top 100 U.S. multinationals. Oil power Exxon Corp, General Motors, oil company Mobil Corp, Ford and IBM were the top five, respectively.

Also ranked were the 100 largest Foreign Investments in the United States, with Royal Dutch/Shell taking another first place. The oil company generated $29 billion in sales through its U.S. subsidiary, Shell Oil.
Forbes said British companies -- not Japanese -- were the biggest investors in the United States.
